```{r}
#| echo: false
#| include: false
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Setup: libraries and the plotting helpers used throughout the deck.
# (Hidden — the same helpers as the Lecture 9 notebook.)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(gridExtra)
})

# Sample ACF with approximate +/- 2/sqrt(T) bands (dashed red); `by` spaces lag labels.
sample_acf_plot <- function(x, L = 20, title = NULL, by = 3) {
  a  <- acf(x, plot = FALSE, lag.max = L)
  df <- data.frame(lag = as.numeric(a$lag)[-1], acf = as.numeric(a$acf)[-1])
  b  <- 2 / sqrt(length(x))
  ggplot(df, aes(lag, acf)) + theme_classic() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, y = 0, yend = acf), linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(b, -b), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, L, by = by)) +
    labs(x = "Lag", y = "Sample ACF", title = title)
}

# Sample PACF with the same +/- 2/sqrt(T) bands (Quenouille's test of the AR order).
sample_pacf_plot <- function(x, L = 20, title = NULL, by = 3) {
  a  <- pacf(x, plot = FALSE, lag.max = L)
  df <- data.frame(lag = as.numeric(a$lag), acf = as.numeric(a$acf))
  b  <- 2 / sqrt(length(x))
  ggplot(df, aes(lag, acf)) + theme_classic() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, y = 0, yend = acf), linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(b, -b), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, L, by = by)) +
    labs(x = "Lag", y = "Sample PACF", title = title)
}
```

# Roadmap {.center}

::: {.incremental}
- **From data to model**: the Box–Jenkins cycle
- **Identification**: the sample ACF and PACF and their sampling distributions
- **Portmanteau tests**: Box–Pierce vs Ljung–Box
- **Method of moments**: Yule–Walker for AR, and why MA models resist it
- **Least squares**: OLS for AR, its finite-sample bias, and CSS for ARMA
:::

# From data to model {background-color="#1b3a6b"}

## Known parameters → estimated parameters {.smaller}

Lectures 6–8 treated the ARMA parameters as **known**: every ACF, PACF and impulse
response was a population object. In practice, we observe **one realization**. Box-Jenkins methodology outlines the process of modelling using observed data.


::: {.keybox}
**The Box–Jenkins cycle**

1. **Identification** — use the sample ACF/PACF to shortlist candidate orders $(p,q)$.
2. **Estimation** — fit each candidate (moments, least squares, ML, Bayesian); compare with information criteria.
3. **Diagnostic checking** — do the residuals look like white noise? If not, back to step 1.
4. **Forecasting and evaluation** — forecast with the accepted model; judge it out of sample.
:::

::: {.callout-ts}
All series here are **stationary**. Unit roots, differencing and ARIMA models come in a later lecture.
:::

## The R toolkit {.smaller}

Everything uses base-R `stats`:

| Function | Job |
|:---|:---|
| `acf()`, `pacf()` | sample correlograms |
| `Box.test()` | Box–Pierce and Ljung–Box portmanteau tests |
| `ar.yw()`, `ar.ols()` | Yule–Walker and least-squares AR estimation |
| `arima(..., method = "CSS")` | conditional sum of squares for ARMA |
| `arima(..., method = "ML")` | exact Gaussian maximum likelihood |

::: {.callout-ts}
**R convention.** `arima()` reports the **mean** $\mu$ under the label
`intercept`, not the constant $c$; recover $c=\mu(1-\phi_1-\cdots-\phi_p)$.
Its MA polynomial is $1+\beta_1L+\cdots+\beta_qL^q$ — the same sign convention as ours.
:::

# Identification: the sample correlogram {background-color="#1b3a6b"}

## Sample moments {.smaller}

The population moments are estimated by their **sample analogues**:

$$
\bar y=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^{T}y_t,
\qquad
\hat\gamma_j=\frac1T\sum_{t=j+1}^{T}(y_t-\bar y)(y_{t-j}-\bar y),
\qquad
\hat\rho_j=\frac{\hat\gamma_j}{\hat\gamma_0}.
$$

- The divisor is $T$, **not** $T-j$. This shrinks $\hat\gamma_j$ slightly towards
  zero at long lags, but guarantees that $\hat\Gamma_p=[\hat\gamma_{|i-j|}]$ is
  **positive definite** — the reason Yule–Walker always delivers a stationary AR.
- Long lags rest on few pairs of observations: inspect lags up to about $T/4$.

::: {.keybox}
The **sample PACF** $\hat\phi_{jj}$ is the last coefficient in the regression of
$y_t$ on $y_{t-1},\dots,y_{t-j}$ — equivalently, it comes from the $\hat\rho_j$ by
the **Durbin–Levinson recursion**.
:::

## How large is "large"? Sampling distributions {.smaller}

**White noise.** If $Y_t$ is i.i.d. with finite variance, for each $j\ge1$
$$
\hat\rho_j\;\overset{a}{\sim}\;N\!\left(0,\tfrac1T\right),
$$
asymptotically independent across lags $\Rightarrow$ 95% bands $\pm2/\sqrt T$.

**MA($q$): Bartlett's formula.** Beyond the cut-off,
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\rho_j)\approx\frac1T\Big(1+2\sum_{i=1}^{q}\rho_i^2\Big),\qquad j>q .
$$
The bands **widen with $q$** — a sequential test of the MA order (`acf(x, ci.type = "ma")`).

**AR($p$): Quenouille's result.**
$$
\hat\phi_{jj}\;\overset{a}{\sim}\;N\!\left(0,\tfrac1T\right),\qquad j>p,
$$
so $\pm2/\sqrt T$ bands on the **sample PACF** test the AR order directly.

## Two cautions {.smaller}

::: {.callout-ts}
1. **Multiple testing.** With 20 lags and 5% bands, about **one** spike will cross
   the bands by chance even for white noise.
2. **Correlation across lags.** Sample autocorrelations of a dependent series are
   correlated with one another, so a sample ACF looks *smoother*, with longer
   waves, than its population counterpart.
:::

> **Do not chase isolated spikes at long, uninterpretable lags.**

## Hands on: SACF and SPACF {.smaller}

We draw (a) **white noise** and (b) an **MA(1) with $\beta=0.7$**, both with $T=100$.

> **Predict:**
>
> 1. For white noise, roughly how many of the first 20 sample autocorrelations
>    should cross $\pm2/\sqrt{T}=\pm0.2$?
> 2. For the MA(1), $\rho_1=\beta/(1+\beta^2)=0.47$. How much wider are Bartlett's
>    bands for lags $j>1$ than the naive $\pm0.2$?
> 3. Which of the four panels should show a **decaying** pattern?

## R — white noise vs MA(1) correlograms {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5.4
set.seed(123)
T  <- 100
wn <- rnorm(T)
ma <- arima.sim(model = list(ma = 0.7), n = T)

rho1     <- 0.7 / (1 + 0.7^2)
bartlett <- 2 * sqrt((1 + 2 * rho1^2) / T)
cat(sprintf("Naive band: +/- %.3f   Bartlett band for j > 1: +/- %.3f\n", 2 / sqrt(T), bartlett))
cat("White-noise lags outside +/- 2/sqrt(T):",
    sum(abs(acf(wn, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 20)$acf[-1]) > 2 / sqrt(T)), "of 20\n")

g_ma <- sample_acf_plot(ma, title = "Sample ACF: MA(1), beta = 0.7") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(bartlett, -bartlett), linetype = "dotted", colour = "blue")
grid.arrange(sample_acf_plot(wn,  title = "Sample ACF: white noise"),
             sample_pacf_plot(wn, title = "Sample PACF: white noise"),
             g_ma,
             sample_pacf_plot(ma, title = "Sample PACF: MA(1), beta = 0.7"),
             ncol = 2)
```

## Reading the graphs {.smaller}

- **White noise:** none of the 20 sample autocorrelations crosses the bands in this
  draw (lags 12 and 14 come close). One crossing in twenty would have been
  entirely normal.
- **MA(1) ACF:** one large spike at lag 1 — **0.32**, well below the population
  value 0.47, a reminder of sampling noise at $T=100$ — then inside the bands,
  apart from an isolated spike at lag 20 that just reaches Bartlett's band:
  exactly the kind of long lag *not* to chase.
- **MA(1) PACF:** a positive spike, then a negative one, dying out — the
  alternating decay of an MA(1) with $\beta>0$, read through sampling noise.

::: {.keybox}
Bartlett's bands (dotted blue) are **20% wider** than the naive ones here
($\pm0.240$ vs $\pm0.200$). With several large $\hat\rho_i$ the correction matters more.
:::

## Portmanteau tests: Box–Pierce and Ljung–Box {.smaller}

Test the first $K$ autocorrelations **jointly**, $H_0:\rho_1=\cdots=\rho_K=0$:

$$
Q_{BP}(K)=T\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat\rho_k^{\,2},
\qquad
Q_{LB}(K)=T(T+2)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\hat\rho_k^{\,2}}{T-k}.
$$

Both $\overset{a}{\sim}\chi^2(K)$ under $H_0$. The Ljung–Box weights
$(T+2)/(T-k)>1$ correct Box–Pierce, whose $\chi^2$ approximation is poor in small
samples.

::: {.keybox}
**On residuals the degrees of freedom change.** For the residuals of an
estimated ARMA($p,q$), the $p+q$ coefficients absorb part of the autocorrelation:
$$
Q(K)\;\overset{a}{\sim}\;\chi^2(K-p-q)
\qquad(\texttt{Box.test(e, lag = K, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = p + q)}).
$$
:::

**Choosing $K$.** Small $K$ lacks power at longer lags; large $K$ dilutes the test.
Common choices: $K\approx10$ (non-seasonal), $K\approx2s$ (seasonal, period $s$).
Reporting several $K$ is good practice.

## Predict before you simulate: test size {.smaller}

We generate **2000 white-noise samples** of length $T=50$ and test with $K=10$ at
the 5% level.

> **Predict:** which test should reject close to **5%** of the time — and which
> less often? Then: what happens when we apply Ljung–Box to an AR(1) with
> $\phi=0.5$?

## R — size and power of the portmanteau tests {.smaller}

```{r}
# Size under white noise (T = 50, K = 10, nominal 5%)
set.seed(123)
reject <- replicate(2000, {
  e <- rnorm(50)
  c(BoxPierce = Box.test(e, lag = 10, type = "Box-Pierce")$p.value < 0.05,
    LjungBox  = Box.test(e, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value  < 0.05)
})
round(rowMeans(reject), 3)

# Power: the same test applied to an AR(1) with phi = 0.5
set.seed(123)
Box.test(arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.5), n = 100), lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")
```

## Reading the output {.smaller}

- **Ljung–Box** rejects about **5%** of the time under the null (0.052), as it should.
- **Box–Pierce** rejects only about **half** as often (0.026) — it is
  *undersized* at $T=50$.
- Against a genuinely dependent AR(1) series, the Ljung–Box statistic is enormous
  ($Q=53.7$ on 10 df, $p\approx5\times10^{-8}$).

> **This is why software and practice default to Ljung–Box.**

## An identification checklist {.smaller}

::: {.keybox}
1. **Plot the series.** Look for trends, breaks, outliers, changing variance and seasonality.
2. **Transform if necessary.** Logs or square roots stabilize a variance that grows
   with the level; differencing removes stochastic trends (later lecture).
3. **Compute the sample ACF and PACF** and compare with the fingerprint table of Lectures 6–8.
4. **Shortlist two to four candidates**, favouring small models (**parsimony**).
5. **Carry all candidates into estimation**; let information criteria, diagnostics
   and out-of-sample performance decide.
:::

::: {.callout-ts}
Mixed ARMA models are hard to separate by eye: **both** the ACF and the PACF decay.
:::

# Estimation I: the method of moments {background-color="#1b3a6b"}

## The estimation problem {.smaller}

For an ARMA($p,q$) we must estimate
$\boldsymbol\theta=(c,\;\phi_1,\dots,\phi_p,\;\beta_1,\dots,\beta_q,\;\sigma^2)'$.
Three features make this harder than cross-section regression:

- **Dependence.** The joint density of the sample is not the product of the marginals.
- **Lagged regressors are not strictly exogenous.** $Y_{t-1}$ is uncorrelated with
  $\varepsilon_t$ but correlated with $\varepsilon_{t-1},\varepsilon_{t-2},\dots$ —
  this biases least squares in finite samples.
- **MA terms are unobserved.** Lagged shocks must be reconstructed from the data,
  making estimation nonlinear.

| Approach | Idea | Natural for |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Method of moments (Yule–Walker) | match population and sample autocovariances | pure AR |
| Least squares (OLS, CSS) | minimize squared one-step errors, conditioning on initial values | AR (OLS); ARMA (CSS) |
| Exact maximum likelihood | maximize the full Gaussian joint density | any ARMA |
| Bayesian | likelihood × prior → posterior | any ARMA; small samples |

## The Yule–Walker equations {.smaller}

Multiply $X_t=\phi_1X_{t-1}+\cdots+\phi_pX_{t-p}+\varepsilon_t$ by $X_{t-j}$,
$j=1,\dots,p$, and take expectations:

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
\gamma_0 & \gamma_1 & \cdots & \gamma_{p-1}\\
\gamma_1 & \gamma_0 & \cdots & \gamma_{p-2}\\
\vdots & & \ddots & \vdots\\
\gamma_{p-1} & \gamma_{p-2} & \cdots & \gamma_0
\end{bmatrix}}_{\Gamma_p}
\begin{bmatrix}\phi_1\\ \vdots\\ \phi_p\end{bmatrix}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\gamma_1\\ \vdots\\ \gamma_p\end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol\gamma_p},
\qquad
\sigma^2=\gamma_0-\boldsymbol\phi'\boldsymbol\gamma_p .
$$

Replacing population by sample moments gives the **Yule–Walker estimator**

$$
\boxed{\;\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}_{YW}=\hat\Gamma_p^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}_p,
\qquad
\hat\sigma^2=\hat\gamma_0-\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}'\hat{\boldsymbol\gamma}_p,
\qquad
\hat c=\bar y\,(1-\hat\phi_1-\cdots-\hat\phi_p).\;}
$$

For an AR(1), $\hat\phi=\hat\rho_1$. For an AR(2):
$$
\hat\phi_1=\frac{\hat\rho_1(1-\hat\rho_2)}{1-\hat\rho_1^2},
\qquad
\hat\phi_2=\frac{\hat\rho_2-\hat\rho_1^2}{1-\hat\rho_1^2}.
$$

## Properties of Yule–Walker {.smaller}

::: {.keybox}
- **Closed form**, no iteration.
- $\hat\Gamma_p$ positive definite $\Rightarrow$ $\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}_{YW}$ is **always stationary**.
- $\sqrt T(\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}_{YW}-\boldsymbol\phi)\overset{d}{\to}N(\mathbf 0,\;\sigma^2\Gamma_p^{-1})$ —
  the same as maximum likelihood, so YW is **asymptotically efficient for pure AR**.
  For an AR(1), $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\phi)\approx(1-\phi^2)/T$.
- The last coefficient $\hat\phi_{pp}$ **is** the sample PACF at lag $p$.
:::

::: {.callout-ts}
In small samples YW is **biased towards zero**, most severely when roots are close
to the unit circle.
:::

> **Predict:** we simulate an AR(2) with $(\phi_1,\phi_2)=(0.5,0.25)$, $T=250$.
> Will the matrix form, the AR(2) formulas, `ar.yw()` and the lag-2 sample PACF
> agree — and on what?

## R — Yule–Walker by hand {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(2024)
y_ar2 <- arima.sim(model = list(ar = c(0.5, 0.25)), n = 250)

g      <- acf(y_ar2, type = "covariance", plot = FALSE, lag.max = 2)$acf[, 1, 1]  # gamma_0..gamma_2
Gam    <- matrix(c(g[1], g[2], g[2], g[1]), 2, 2)
phi_yw <- solve(Gam, g[2:3])
s2_yw  <- g[1] - sum(phi_yw * g[2:3])
r      <- g / g[1]

cat("True (phi1, phi2)            : 0.5000 0.2500\n")
cat("Yule-Walker, matrix form     :", round(phi_yw, 4), "  sigma2 =", round(s2_yw, 4), "\n")
cat("Yule-Walker, AR(2) formulas  :", round(c(r[2] * (1 - r[3]) / (1 - r[2]^2),
                                            (r[3] - r[2]^2) / (1 - r[2]^2)), 4), "\n")
cat("ar.yw()                      :", round(ar.yw(y_ar2, order.max = 2, aic = FALSE)$ar, 4), "\n")
cat("Sample PACF at lag 2         :", round(pacf(y_ar2, plot = FALSE)$acf[2], 4), "  (= phi_22)\n")
cat("Asymptotic s.e.              :", round(sqrt(diag(s2_yw * solve(Gam) / length(y_ar2))), 4), "\n")
```

## What you should see {.smaller}

- All three routes give **identical** estimates, $(\hat\phi_1,\hat\phi_2)=(0.522,\,0.172)$:
  the matrix form, the closed-form AR(2) formulas and `ar.yw()` are the same calculation.
- The lag-2 **sample PACF equals $\hat\phi_{2}$** exactly (0.1716).
- $\hat\phi_2=0.17$ is about **1.3 standard errors** (s.e. $\approx0.062$) below the
  true 0.25 — sampling noise, consistent with the downward small-sample pull.

::: {.keybox}
**Yule–Walker and the PACF are the same calculation.** Identifying an AR order
with the sample PACF and estimating it by Yule–Walker use exactly the same numbers.
:::

## MA models resist the method of moments {.smaller}

For an MA(1), $\rho_1=\beta/(1+\beta^2)$. Matching moments gives
$\hat\rho_1\beta^2-\beta+\hat\rho_1=0$, whose **invertible** root is

$$
\hat\beta_{MM}=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4\hat\rho_1^{\,2}}}{2\hat\rho_1}.
$$

::: {.callout-ts}
A real solution exists **only if $|\hat\rho_1|\le0.5$**, because $|\rho_1|\le0.5$
for every MA(1). When $\beta$ is large, sampling noise often pushes $|\hat\rho_1|$
above 0.5 — and the estimator **does not exist**. Even when it exists it is
inefficient: moment estimators are mainly useful as **starting values** for
likelihood-based estimation.
:::

> **Predict:** for $\beta=0.9$ (so $\rho_1=0.497$) and $T=100$, in what share of
> samples does $\hat\beta_{MM}$ fail to exist?

## R — how often does the moment estimator fail? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.8
set.seed(123)
rho1_hat <- replicate(2000, {
  y <- arima.sim(model = list(ma = 0.9), n = 100)
  acf(y, plot = FALSE)$acf[2]
})
cat(sprintf("Share of samples with |rho1_hat| > 0.5 (no real solution): %.1f%%\n",
            100 * mean(abs(rho1_hat) > 0.5)))

ggplot(data.frame(r = rho1_hat), aes(r)) + theme_classic() +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey70", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = expression(hat(rho)[1]), y = "Count",
       title = "Lag-1 sample autocorrelation, MA(1) with beta = 0.9",
       subtitle = "Right of the dashed line the moment equation has no real solution")
```

## Interpretation {.smaller}

- In about **a third** of the samples (36.4%) the moment estimator **does not
  exist at all** — even though the true model is a perfectly well-behaved,
  invertible MA(1).
- The true $\rho_1=0.497$ sits right at the boundary, so the sampling
  distribution of $\hat\rho_1$ straddles 0.5.

::: {.keybox}
Likelihood-based estimators have no such problem: they use the **whole
autocorrelation structure**, not a single moment.
:::

$$\boxed{\text{well-behaved model}\not\Rightarrow\text{well-behaved moment estimator}}$$

# Estimation II: least squares {background-color="#1b3a6b"}

## OLS for AR($p$) {.smaller}

Conditioning on the first $p$ observations, an AR($p$) is a linear regression for
$t=p+1,\dots,T$:

$$
Y_t=\mathbf x_t'\mathbf b+\varepsilon_t,
\qquad
\mathbf x_t=(1,\;Y_{t-1},\dots,Y_{t-p})',
\qquad
\mathbf b=(c,\;\phi_1,\dots,\phi_p)',
$$

$$
\hat{\mathbf b}_{OLS}=\Big(\sum_{t=p+1}^{T}\mathbf x_t\mathbf x_t'\Big)^{-1}\sum_{t=p+1}^{T}\mathbf x_tY_t,
\qquad
\hat\sigma^2=\frac{1}{T-p}\sum_{t=p+1}^{T}\hat\varepsilon_t^{\,2}.
$$

::: {.keybox}
$E(\varepsilon_t\mid\mathbf x_t)=0$ (**contemporaneous exogeneity**) $\Rightarrow$
OLS is **consistent and asymptotically normal**; the usual OLS standard errors are
valid in large samples.
:::

## …but biased in finite samples {.smaller}

The regressors are **not strictly exogenous**: $\varepsilon_t$ feeds into the
future regressors $Y_t,Y_{t+1},\dots$, so $E(\hat{\mathbf b})\ne\mathbf b$ in
finite samples. For an AR(1) with an estimated intercept (Kendall 1954; Marriott
and Pope 1954):

$$
E(\hat\phi_{OLS})-\phi\;\approx\;-\frac{1+3\phi}{T}.
$$

::: {.callout-ts}
The bias is **downward** and **grows with persistence**: OLS **understates
persistence**, so estimated half-lives are too short.
:::

> **Predict:** we draw 2000 samples from an AR(1) with $\phi=0.9$ at
> $T=25,50,100,250$ and estimate $\phi$ by OLS. What sign does the bias have?
> Roughly how large is it at $T=25$?

## R — Monte Carlo bias of OLS {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.6
set.seed(123)
phi  <- 0.9
Ts   <- c(25, 50, 100, 250)
ests <- lapply(Ts, function(T) replicate(2000, {
  y <- arima.sim(model = list(ar = phi), n = T)
  coef(lm(y[-1] ~ y[-T]))[2]
}))

bias_tab <- data.frame(T = Ts, mean_phi_hat = sapply(ests, mean),
                       bias = sapply(ests, mean) - phi, approx_bias = -(1 + 3 * phi) / Ts)
print(round(bias_tab, 4), row.names = FALSE)

dens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 3), function(i)
  data.frame(phi_hat = ests[[i]], T = paste("T =", Ts[i]))))
ggplot(dens, aes(phi_hat, linetype = T)) + theme_classic() + geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = phi, colour = "red") +
  labs(x = expression(hat(phi)[OLS]), y = "Density", linetype = NULL,
       title = "Sampling distribution of OLS in an AR(1) with phi = 0.9 (red line)")
```

## Reading the output {.smaller}

| $T$ | mean $\hat\phi$ | bias | $-(1+3\phi)/T$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 25 | 0.730 | $-0.170$ | $-0.148$ |
| 50 | 0.818 | $-0.082$ | $-0.074$ |
| 100 | 0.860 | $-0.040$ | $-0.037$ |
| 250 | 0.884 | $-0.016$ | $-0.015$ |

- The bias is **negative at every $T$** and roughly **halves each time $T$ doubles**,
  as the approximation predicts.
- At $T=25$ the typical estimate is about **0.73**, not 0.9, and the distribution
  has a long **left tail**.

::: {.keybox}
**Real-world anchor.** With quarterly macro data, 25 years is $T=100$ — where
the bias is still about $-0.04$: enough to shorten an estimated **half-life** noticeably.
:::

## Conditional least squares for ARMA($p,q$) {.smaller}

With MA terms the lagged shocks are unobserved, so build them **recursively**. For
trial values of $(c,\boldsymbol\phi,\boldsymbol\beta)$,

$$
\varepsilon_t(\boldsymbol\phi,\boldsymbol\beta)=Y_t-c-\sum_{i=1}^{p}\phi_iY_{t-i}-\sum_{j=1}^{q}\beta_j\,\varepsilon_{t-j}(\boldsymbol\phi,\boldsymbol\beta),
\qquad t=p+1,\dots,T,
$$

with pre-sample shocks set to zero.

::: {.keybox}
**Conditional sum of squares (CSS)** minimizes
$S(c,\boldsymbol\phi,\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2$. It is nonlinear in
$\boldsymbol\beta$, so it is solved numerically: `arima(y, order = c(p, 0, q), method = "CSS")`.
:::

::: {.callout-ts}
**Invertibility is what makes CSS work.** An error in the arbitrary start
$\varepsilon_p=0$ enters $\varepsilon_t$ multiplied by $(-\beta)^{t-p}$ in an
MA(1). It dies out only if $|\beta|<1$. Near the boundary CSS performs poorly and
**exact maximum likelihood** is preferred.
:::

# Recap {background-color="#1b3a6b"}

## Key takeaways {.smaller}

::: {.keybox}
- **Box–Jenkins:** identify → estimate → check → forecast, and loop back when the residuals say so.
- **Sampling bands:** $\pm2/\sqrt T$ under white noise; **Bartlett** widens ACF bands beyond an MA($q$) cut-off; **Quenouille** justifies $\pm2/\sqrt T$ on the PACF beyond an AR($p$).
- **Don't chase** isolated spikes at long lags — about one in twenty crosses by chance.
- **Ljung–Box** has the right size in small samples; Box–Pierce is undersized. On residuals use $\chi^2(K-p-q)$.
- **Yule–Walker** is closed form, always stationary, asymptotically efficient for pure AR — and identical to the PACF calculation.
- **MA moment estimators** can fail to exist ($|\hat\rho_1|>0.5$); use them only as starting values.
- **OLS for AR** is consistent but biased downward by about $-(1+3\phi)/T$: it **understates persistence**.
- **CSS** extends least squares to ARMA, and relies on **invertibility**.
:::

## Exercises {.smaller}

1. **Reading a correlogram.** For $T=150$ the first five sample autocorrelations
   are $0.42,\,0.08,\,-0.05,\,0.04,\,-0.10$. (a) Which are individually significant
   using $\pm2/\sqrt T$? (b) Assuming an MA(1), use Bartlett's formula to test
   $\rho_2=0$. (c) Compute the Ljung–Box statistic $Q(5)$ and test white noise.
   (d) What model would you propose?
2. **Yule–Walker by hand.** For an AR(2), $\hat\gamma_0=2$, $\hat\rho_1=0.6$,
   $\hat\rho_2=0.45$. Compute $\hat\phi_1$, $\hat\phi_2$ and $\hat\sigma^2$. Is the
   estimated model stationary? Does it have complex roots?
3. **The method of moments for an MA(1).** (a) For $\hat\rho_1=0.4$, find both
   solutions of the moment equation and choose the invertible one. (b) Explain why
   there is no solution for $\hat\rho_1=0.55$. (c) What does this suggest about the
   true $\beta$, and what would you do in practice?

## Suggested reading {.smaller}

- Hamilton, J. D. (1994), *Time Series Analysis*, Princeton University Press: Ch. 4 (§4.8 on Wold's decomposition and the Box–Jenkins philosophy).
- Enders, W. (2015), *Applied Econometric Time Series*, 4th ed., Wiley: Ch. 2.
- Brockwell, P. J. and Davis, R. A. (2016), *Introduction to Time Series and Forecasting*, 3rd ed., Springer: Ch. 5.
- Box, G. E. P., Jenkins, G. M., Reinsel, G. C. and Ljung, G. M. (2015), *Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control*, 5th ed., Wiley — the original methodology.
- Hyndman, R. J. and Athanasopoulos, G., *Forecasting: Principles and Practice*, 3rd ed., free online at [otexts.com/fpp3](https://otexts.com/fpp3/).
- Diebold, F. X., *Elements of Forecasting*, 4th ed. ([free PDF on the author's site](https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~fdiebold/Teaching221/BookPhotocopy.pdf)).
- **Original papers:** Yule (1927) on sunspots and autoregression; Box and Pierce (1970) and Ljung and Box (1978) on portmanteau tests.

## R quick reference {.smaller}

| Task | Function | Notes |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Sample ACF / PACF | `acf(x)`, `pacf(x)` | `acf(x, ci.type = "ma")` draws Bartlett bands |
| Portmanteau test | `Box.test(e, lag = K, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = p + q)` | set `fitdf` when testing residuals |
| Yule–Walker / OLS for AR | `ar.yw(x, order.max = p, aic = FALSE)`, `ar.ols()` | `aic = TRUE` chooses $p$ by AIC |
| CSS / exact ML for ARMA | `arima(x, order = c(p, 0, q), method = "CSS")` / `"ML"` | `intercept` is the mean $\mu$ |
